title: Medical questions
hook: modern fiqh on transplants, IVF, end of life, where scholars reason and differ

segments.voice: Yesterday, animals' rights, and your line: they have rights. A camel complained in a garden, and the Prophet heard it.

Brain-dead. A doctor says the word to a family in a hospital corridor late at night, about their father, and gently asks about donating his kidneys. A few floors up, a young couple is talking with a fertility clinic. At the end of the hall, a grandmother's machines keep her body going after her doctors say they can no longer help. None of this is in the Qur'an by name. The jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba never saw a ventilator. Yet a Muslim family in that corridor might call a scholar and ask: what does the law say?
screen: `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR AT NIGHT.` → `DONATION, FERTILITY, MACHINES.` → `NONE OF IT NAMED IN THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Start with medicine itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Seeking treatment is part of the tradition. Then the method. Scholars look for a text that speaks to the new question, reason by analogy from cases that do appear, and weigh the purposes of the law, which we'll meet in two days. That effort is called ijtihad. Organ transplants: some fiqh councils have allowed donation, within limits, reading it through the verse in surah five that whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of humankind. Other scholars have objected, out of reverence for the body after death, which the tradition protects. Fertility: Sunni councils have allowed IVF between a married couple, using their own egg and sperm, and refused a third party's; some Shia authorities have reasoned more widely, allowing some forms of donation. Same texts, different reasoning, both careful. End of life: the same verse likens killing one soul to killing all humankind, and scholars read it as forbidding a deliberately ended life. Some allow stopping treatment that only prolongs dying, when doctors judge there is no hope of recovery, and brain death is still argued. So the answer is often not one fatwa but a few, each showing its reasoning. That isn't confusion. It's an old method, honestly applied.
screen: `GOD SENT A CURE WITH EVERY DISEASE.` · `IJTIHAD: TEXT, ANALOGY, PURPOSE.` · `TRANSPLANTS AND IVF: COUNCILS DIFFER.` · `END OF LIFE: NO KILLING, SOME LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Think of one medical decision someone you love has faced, or might, and name it plainly: donation, a treatment, a hard ending. Ask today's three questions gently: is there a text, is there a case like it, what is the law trying to protect? Then hold the person and the question side by side. If a hard ending is close for you, or you're thinking of ending your own life, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Medical questions. New cases in medicine, from transplants to fertility to the end of life, that scholars answer by reasoning from the old sources, and on which they sometimes differ. Today's word.
Your line: old method, new questions. An old method can still reach a hospital corridor. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslim patients and families facing questions about transplants, fertility treatment or end-of-life care may ask a trusted scholar or consult the rulings of fiqh councils, which reason from the Qur'an, the hadith and the purposes of the law.

chat.meaning: New questions get ijtihad. Some councils allow donation, citing saving a life; other scholars object out of reverence for the body.

ijtihad.meaning: the effort of reasoning to answer a new legal question

fatwa.meaning: a scholar's answer to a question about the law

Baghdad.meaning: a city in Iraq, home to early jurists

Cordoba.meaning: a city in Spain, home to Muslim jurists long ago

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5678 (a cure sent down for every disease)

notes: 5:32 paraphrased; Pickthall's wording is 'whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind'; not quoted to be safe.
Transplants: 'many fiqh councils have allowed' (e.g. OIC Islamic Fiqh Academy 1988, Saudi Council of Senior Scholars); confirm. Objectors exist; confirm fair.
IVF: Sunni councils (e.g. Al-Azhar) allow within marriage, no third party; some Shia authorities (e.g. a fatwa attributed to Ayatollah Khamenei) allowed donor gametes. Confirm, and whether to name.
End of life: euthanasia forbidden; withdrawing futile treatment allowed by some (e.g. OIC academy rulings): confirm. Brain death debate open.
'Jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba' is illustrative; hospital scene is illustrative.
